title: The Nineteenth Floor
subtitle: Armistice Day, a Penthouse in the Fog, and Everyone Who Wants the Crane in One Room

setting.name: San Francisco, Friday 11 November (Armistice Day) to Saturday 12 November 1938
setting.description: The last day. Dolan's deadline is midnight. Corinne Marsh sails for Honolulu at nine tomorrow morning with $38,000 of somebody else's bonds in a vanity case. Mick Larrabee believes the party has his diamonds and has sent to Los Angeles for a man who settles such things. Lonnie Pruitt is trying to get on a bus to Lodi. And at ten tonight, on the nineteenth floor of the Mark Hopkins, in a penthouse the hotel means to turn into a cocktail lounge next year, Ambrose Pellingham is giving a party to settle the matter of the crane among all interested parties: the collector who holds the murder weapon, the widow who used it, the waterfront boss who wants his money, the refugee who wants her family's life back, the agency whose partner is dead, and, if the party has earned his trust, a homicide lieutenant listening behind a bedroom door. Everyone in the room holds something. By morning, everyone will have traded it.
setting.atmosphere: The day is bright and cold and patriotic: flags on Market Street, the Armistice Day parade at eleven, veterans of 1918 marching in their old caps with their medals on, a band playing 'Over There', two minutes' silence at the eleventh hour when the streetcars stop and the whole city stands still. Then the fog, which comes in at five and does not lift. The penthouse at night is a lit box nineteen floors above a white sea: Chinese carpets, a fire, a Steinway, a bar trolley, the builders' scaffolding for next year's lounge clamped to the outside of the windows, and through the glass nothing at all, only the fog and the glow of the city under it, and the beam of the Alcatraz light going round. It is a drawing-room scene with guns in the coats. Let it be talky, and tense, and let the talk be the fight until it is not.

keyLocations.name: The Penthouse, the Mark Hopkins
keyLocations.description: The whole nineteenth floor: a great drawing room with windows on three sides, a dining room, two bedrooms, a service pantry with its own lift, and a door onto the roof stairs. Builders' scaffolding is clamped outside the west and north windows, where the hotel's contractors have begun the alterations for next year's cocktail lounge; one window in the drawing room has been taken out and boarded with a hinged panel for their access.
features: The drawing room: a fire, a Steinway, a long sofa, Pellingham's great armchair, a lacquer side table where he means the crane to stand
Pellingham's bedroom: a wardrobe of dove-grey suits, a dressing table, and on the top shelf of the closet, a round black hatbox from Lock of St. James's
The service pantry and its lift, by which a man can come up from the kitchens unannounced
The scaffolding outside: planks, pipes, a rope hoist, wet with fog, nineteen floors over California Street
encounters: Ambrose Pellingham, host, and his bodyguard Mr. Rudd (Bodyguard)
Lonnie Pruitt (Hired Gun stats), on the sofa arm, a glass of milk in his hand
Corinne Marsh, in grey, the silver fox, and a small blue leather vanity case on her knee
Mick Larrabee (Waterfront Boss) with Tiny Mulcahy (Mob Lieutenant), and later Larrabee's man from Los Angeles, Mr. Gray (The Professional), who comes up the service lift
Magda Ehrlich, if she comes; she will, unless the party forbids it, and even then she might
secrets: CLUE G8: in the hatbox, wrapped in one of Pellingham's silk scarves, is a Colt .32 automatic, Model 1903, serial 482117, with six rounds left in its eight-round magazine: she loaded it full that evening from the box in the bedside drawer, and fired twice. Dr. Lindqvist, given the gun and the two Tallow Alley casings, will match the ejector and firing-pin marks under her comparison microscope by Saturday noon.
Pellingham's settlement (see Act 2) is a real offer and he will honour it. He has $10,000 in the suite's safe to make it work.
The hinged boarding over the drawing-room window opens onto the scaffold. Anyone desperate enough to run that way can reach the roof stairs along forty feet of wet planks, or the rope hoist.

keyLocations.name: Market Street on Armistice Day
keyLocations.description: The parade from the Ferry Building to the Civic Center at eleven: veterans' posts, a navy band from the Yerba Buena training station, Boy Scouts, the American Legion, nurses from 1918 in their capes, the mayor's car, flags on every lamp standard. At eleven exactly, the streetcars and cable cars stop and the city keeps two minutes' silence.
features: Crowds ten deep on the sidewalks, which is very good for being followed and very good for losing someone
The reviewing stand at the Civic Center
encounters: Tiny Mulcahy and two Dockside Goons, sent to deliver Larrabee's ultimatum in the crowd
Augie Brodzinski's old company from the 91st Division, marching, if Augie is in the party
secrets: Larrabee's ultimatum: 'Mick says bring the bird and what was in it to the party tonight, and he'll call it square at six thousand. Or he's got a man coming up from Los Angeles on the Daylight who doesn't argue.'

During the two minutes' silence, Tiny Mulcahy, an old soldier's son, takes his hat off with everyone else, and the party can talk to him as a man rather than as Larrabee's: Persuasion DC 13 gets a promise that he will not start anything tonight. He keeps it.

keyLocations.name: The Greyhound Depot, Seventh and Market
keyLocations.description: The bus depot: a waiting room of benches, a lunch counter, a newsstand, loudspeakers calling the Stockton and Sacramento coaches, and the 3:15 for Lodi.
features: The ticket window, the lockers, the coach bays out back
A telephone booth by the lunch counter
encounters: Lonnie Pruitt, with a cardboard suitcase and a one-way ticket to Lodi, at 2:45
Mr. Rudd (Bodyguard), sent by Pellingham to bring him back, at 3:00
secrets: CLUE G7 (early route): if the party reaches Lonnie before Rudd does and convinces him (Persuasion DC 14, advantage if they bring his hat, or Rose Fong, or a promise of Dolan's protection), he tells them everything: Pellingham sent him to follow Ned; he waited on the Hall of Justice steps; he heard the shots and saw a lady in a pale fur run out of the alley and drop something in an ash can; he took it out, it was a pistol, warm; he lost his hat running; he gave the pistol to Pellingham at midnight, and Pellingham put it in the hatbox. He will say it to Dolan. He will not say it in front of Pellingham unless the party is standing beside him.
If Rudd gets Lonnie first, Lonnie is in the penthouse at ten, and the party must win him there.

keyLocations.name: The Hall of Justice
keyLocations.description: Dolan's office on the third floor, Hattie Lindqvist's morgue in the basement with its comparison microscope, and the cells upstairs where Wally Kerrigan, if the party gave him up, is sitting on a bunk in his shirtsleeves.
features: Dolan's desk, a warrant for Cass Delaney already typed and unsigned in the top drawer
Hattie's comparison microscope: two eyepieces, a bridge, a bullet on each stage, her cigarette in a beaker
encounters: Dolan, who agrees to a plan, or does not
Kerrigan, in a cell, who knows Larrabee has sent for a man from Los Angeles and will say so for a cigarette and a kind word from someone, because Dolan will not look at him
secrets: Dolan will come to the penthouse, by the service lift, and wait in Pellingham's second bedroom with the door ajar, if the party has been straight with him (Heat 4 or less, or they gave him Kerrigan). Otherwise he arrives at midnight with two uniformed men and the warrant for Cass, and the party must make their case in front of him cold.
Kerrigan: 'Mick's sent for Gray. Out of Los Angeles. Gray doesn't do the talking, he does the other thing. He'll come up the back way.'

keyLocations.name: Pier 35, Saturday Morning
keyLocations.description: The Matson liner at Pier 35, north of the Ferry Building, white and enormous, with streamers and a band on the pier, and passengers going up the gangway at eight for a nine o'clock sailing.
features: The first-class gangway, a purser's table with the passenger list, porters, a florist's cart
Cabin B-14, booked for Mrs. C. J. Marsh
encounters: Corinne Marsh, if she left the penthouse free and with the vanity case
Dolan and two uniformed men, if the party sent them
secrets: This location is only used if Corinne escapes the penthouse. If she does, the last scene of the campaign is the gangway at a quarter to nine, with a band playing 'Aloha Oe' and streamers coming down, and a decision about whether to stop her.

synopsis: Armistice Day. In the morning Larrabee's men deliver an ultimatum in the parade crowd on Market Street, and Kerrigan, in a cell, warns that a man is coming up from Los Angeles. In the afternoon Lonnie Pruitt tries to catch a bus home to Lodi and the party can reach him before Pellingham's bodyguard does. At ten the whole case gathers in Pellingham's penthouse on top of the Mark Hopkins, with the fog against the windows: the collector with the gun in a hatbox, the widow with the bonds in a vanity case, the waterfront boss with his debt, the refugee with her claim, the party with the cracked crane and the case, and perhaps Dolan behind a bedroom door. Pellingham proposes a civilised settlement in which everybody is paid and nobody is hanged. The party can accept it, or lay out the case against Corinne Marsh in front of everyone, break her fourth account, and win Lonnie's testimony and the pistol. Then Larrabee's man from Los Angeles comes up the service lift, Corinne runs for the scaffolding with the vanity case nineteen floors above California Street, and in the end the party must decide what becomes of the bonds, the bird, and the woman who killed Ned Corrigan.
hook: At eleven o'clock on Armistice Day the streetcars on Market Street stop where they are and the cable cars on the hills stop on their cables, and the whole city takes off its hat. In the silence you can hear the flags moving on the lamp standards and a baby crying somewhere on the corner of Fourth Street, and a gull. In the parade, an old man in a 1918 cap stands to attention with tears running into his moustache. Ned used to come and watch this every year; he never said why. When the two minutes are over and the band starts up again, a huge soft-spoken man with a ruined ear is standing next to you with his hat still in his hands. 'Mick says to tell you,' says Tiny Mulcahy, apologetically, 'bring the bird tonight.'

acts.title: Act 1: Armistice Day
acts.description: Friday 11 November, from the parade to nine at night. The ultimatum, the bus depot, and the plan. This act gives the party the chance to find the last witness (G7, Lonnie) before the penthouse, to make an alliance with Dolan, and to decide with Magda what they are walking into.
objectives: Hear Larrabee's ultimatum and, if possible, take the sting out of Tiny Mulcahy
Reach Lonnie Pruitt before Pellingham's bodyguard does
Make a plan with Dolan, or decide not to
Decide, with Magda, what the party will accept tonight

scenes.name: The Two Minutes
scenes.description: Market Street at eleven, the parade, the silence. Tiny Mulcahy delivers Larrabee's ultimatum. If Augie is in the party, his old company marches past and someone shouts his name.
scenes.readAloud: The band strikes up 'Over There' and the old soldiers step off again, not quite in time, with their medals swinging. Tiny Mulcahy turns his hat round and round in his big hands. 'I'll be honest,' he says. 'I don't like it. I don't like the man Mick's sent for. My old man was at the Argonne. He used to say the worst thing in the world is a man who does killing for a wage and enjoys his work.' He puts his hat on. 'Ten o'clock. Bring the bird and what was in it, and Mick calls it square at six thousand. Or Gray comes up the back way.'

skillChecks.success: Tiny promises he will not start anything tonight, and will not let Larrabee's men start anything either, unless someone draws on Larrabee. He keeps his word, and in Act 3 he steps out of the fight.
skillChecks.failure: Tiny is sorry, but he works for Mick. Tonight he does what Mick says.

skillChecks.success: Tiny believes the party has the diamonds. So does Larrabee. Tell them the truth about the empty base and Tiny believes it, which is worth something: Larrabee does not, yet.
skillChecks.failure: Tiny is unreadable, the way large quiet men often are.

scenes.name: The 3:15 for Lodi
scenes.description: The Greyhound depot. Lonnie is on a bench with a cardboard suitcase and a ticket, eating a doughnut he is not tasting. Rudd, Pellingham's bodyguard, arrives at three to bring him back. The party, if they guessed (Pruneau will tell them Lonnie left with a suitcase at two; Rose can find out which bus from the depot's switchboard), can be there first.
scenes.readAloud: Lonnie Pruitt is sitting at the very end of a long bench under the loudspeaker, with a cardboard suitcase between his feet and a new hat on his knees, and he is eating a doughnut in small bites like a child who has been told to finish it. When he sees you he stops chewing. He does not run. He looks at the clock over the ticket window, which says ten to three, and then he looks at the doors to the street, and then he looks at you, and his eyes fill up. 'I knew somebody'd come,' he says. 'I kind of hoped it'd be you.'

skillChecks.success: Lonnie tells the whole story (Clue G7): the steps, the shots, the woman in the pale fur, the ash can, the pistol still warm, the hat lost running, the hatbox. Advantage if the party brings his hat from the printer's shop, or Rose Fong, or a promise from Dolan. He agrees to say it to Dolan, and to say it in the penthouse if one of the party stands next to him.
skillChecks.failure: Lonnie wants to tell you, but he is too frightened of Pellingham, of the cops, of Larrabee, of being hanged. He gets on the bus. He will get off it at Stockton and telephone the agency at seven, and he can be fetched back.

skillChecks.success: When Rudd comes through the doors at three, a party member gets between him and Lonnie. Rudd sizes them up, decides this is not worth a scene in a bus station, and leaves to tell Pellingham. (A fight here is +2 Heat and in front of two hundred people.)
skillChecks.failure: Rudd takes Lonnie by the elbow, firmly, and walks him out. Lonnie looks back once. He will be in the penthouse tonight.

scenes.name: Terms
scenes.description: The agency office, six to nine. Dolan, Magda, Hattie's verdict on the gloves, and Dot's case board. The party decides who goes up the hill tonight, who carries the crane, whether Dolan hides in the bedroom, and what they are willing to trade.
scenes.readAloud: Dot has the case board out of the cupboard and onto the desk, and it covers it: Ned's photograph in the middle, cards and string, VIVIAN MARSH in red pencil with GLOVES, FOX, CABLE CAR, COLT, LETTER, MATSON pinned round her like a cloud, and in the corner a card that says only HATBOX? Magda is sitting in Ned's chair with her coat on. Dolan is standing at the window with his back to all of you, looking down at Market Street, where they are sweeping up the parade. 'I can't take a Nob Hill widow on this,' he says to the glass. 'Not and make it stick. I need the gun and the kid. Get me in that room.'

skillChecks.success: Dolan agrees to come up by the service lift at a quarter to ten and wait in the second bedroom with the door ajar, and not to come out until the party says a word they agree on. If Heat is 5 or more, the DC is 16.
skillChecks.failure: Dolan will come at midnight, through the front door, with two uniformed men and the warrant for Cass in his pocket. The party must have it done by then.

skillChecks.success: Magda, asked what she wants, says it plainly: the bonds in the Bank of America by the 18th, and Mrs. Marsh to pay for Mr. Corrigan. If she must choose, she says, 'my family, and then Mr. Corrigan, and then the crane, and I am ashamed of the order.' She is going tonight whatever the party says. 'It is my family's bird. I will be in the room.'
skillChecks.failure: Magda says only that she is coming.

encounters: Tiny Mulcahy (Mob Lieutenant) and two Dockside Goons in the parade crowd, not a fight unless the party makes one
Mr. Rudd (Bodyguard) at the Greyhound depot, who will not fight in public unless attacked

acts.title: Act 2: Ten O'Clock
acts.description: The penthouse. Everyone arrives; Pellingham sets out the terms; the party makes its case. This act completes the final conclusion, 'Corinne Marsh shot Ned Corrigan with her husband's Colt and Pellingham has kept the gun', with its last two clues (G7 Lonnie's account, if not already given, and G8 the pistol), and presents the moral choice in the form of Pellingham's settlement.
objectives: Get into the room with the crane, and with whoever the party chooses
Lay out the case against Corinne Marsh, in front of everyone
Win Lonnie's testimony in front of Pellingham
Get the pistol out of the hatbox

scenes.name: All Interested Parties
scenes.description: Arrivals. Pellingham receives everyone personally, pours drinks, and seats them like a hostess. Larrabee and Tiny; Corinne with the vanity case; Magda; the party with the cracked crane in a hatbox of their own; Lonnie on the sofa arm with a glass of milk; Rudd by the pantry door. Then Pellingham, standing by the fire, sets out what each person holds, and his terms.
scenes.readAloud: 'Thank you all,' says Mr. Pellingham, 'for coming out on such a night.' He stands by the fire with a glass of Madeira in his beautiful hands, enormous and gracious and absolutely calm, and the fog presses at the windows behind him like an audience. 'Let us be honest, since honesty is so rare and so cheap tonight. Our friends from the agency hold the crane. Mrs. Marsh holds what was in it; that little blue case, I think, madam. Mr. Larrabee holds a debt and a great many large men. Miss Ehrlich holds a claim, and a better one than any of us. And I,' he smiles, 'hold something of the late Mr. Marsh's that would interest the police very much. So. I propose that we all go home richer, and that nobody hangs.'

skillChecks.success: Pellingham means every word of his settlement. He is also, under the courtesy, furious with Corinne for the robbery, and would enjoy seeing her ruined almost as much as he would enjoy the crane. If the party refuses his terms, he will trade the gun to them for the bird and enjoy it.
skillChecks.failure: Pellingham is a pleasant fat man proposing a business arrangement. You know better, but you cannot see what he wants beyond the bird.

skillChecks.success: Larrabee keeps looking at the pantry door and then at his watch. He is expecting someone. Corinne has not let go of the vanity case for a second, and her left hand is resting on its clasp.
skillChecks.failure: Everyone is drinking. Nobody is drunk.

scenes.name: The Settlement
scenes.description: Pellingham's terms, in full: the crane to him. Mr. Larrabee is paid $6,000 by Pellingham, from the safe, tonight, and goes home. The bonds are divided: half to Miss Ehrlich, half to Mrs. Marsh. The agency receives $5,000 from Pellingham for its trouble. And Mrs. Marsh receives back her late husband's property, which Pellingham will place in her hand, and which she may drop off the Hyde Street pier on her way to the boat. Everyone is paid. Ned Corrigan stays dead and nobody answers for him. This is the devil's bargain, and it is a real one.
scenes.readAloud: Pellingham sets out his terms the way a man lays out a hand of patience, one card at a time, and when he has finished there is a long silence in which you can hear the fire and the foghorn on Alcatraz. Larrabee says, 'Six thousand. Tonight.' Pellingham inclines his head. Corinne says nothing at all; she is looking at Magda, and Magda is looking at the floor. 'Nineteen thousand dollars, Miss Ehrlich,' Pellingham says gently. 'I am told the American consul in Lisbon would find it quite sufficient. And it would be in a bank on Monday.' He turns his small kind eyes on you. 'And you, my friends, would have five thousand dollars and your liberty, and Lieutenant Dolan would have, I am afraid, a mystery. I do so dislike violence. Shall we?'

skillChecks.success: Magda is tempted. Nineteen thousand might be enough for the consul. She will not say yes or no for the party; she will say, in a very low voice, 'Mr. Corrigan made a joke about the elevator,' and look at them.
skillChecks.failure: Magda's face gives nothing away. She has had a great deal of practice.

skillChecks.success: If the party refuses and argues it well, Pellingham shrugs, smiles, and amends his offer: 'Then, since you insist on justice, let us make it a simpler trade. The bird for the hatbox.' He means it.
skillChecks.failure: Pellingham regrets that the party is unreasonable, and turns to Corinne to make the deal without them. The party must make their case now, before the hatbox goes into her hands.

scenes.name: The Case
scenes.description: The party lays out the case against Corinne Marsh, in front of everyone. Run this as the classic drawing-room reveal: let the players speak it, clue by clue, and have the room react. Corinne gives her fourth and last account. Lonnie must decide whether to speak in front of Pellingham. The hatbox must be opened.
scenes.readAloud: When you have finished, nobody in the room moves. Corinne Marsh sits very straight on the sofa with the blue vanity case on her knees and the silver fox on her shoulders, and for a long moment she looks like what she was before she married, a singer waiting in the wings for her cue. Then she opens her bag and takes out a cigarette, and holds it up, and looks at the nearest man in the party. It is the first time all week she has waited for someone to light it. 'He put his hand on my arm,' she says. 'Your Mr. Corrigan. He leaned in with his lighter and he said, very kindly, that he'd have to take it to the police if I wouldn't be decent. Decent. I had sixty-three dollars.' The cigarette shakes. 'I only meant to frighten him.'

skillChecks.success: Her fourth account is half true. Ned did lean in to light her cigarette; that is why the fox hairs are on his right sleeve and why the lighter was in his hand. But she let him, and she never lets a man light her cigarettes. She let him close and turned him so that she could fire. She did not mean to frighten him. She had loaded the gun full that evening.
skillChecks.failure: She sounds like a frightened woman who made a terrible mistake. A jury might think so. You are not sure what you think.

skillChecks.success: With a party member standing beside him, Lonnie Pruitt puts down his glass of milk, stands up, and says it in front of Pellingham, Larrabee and everyone: the steps, the shots, the woman in the fur, the ash can, the gun, the hatbox. (Clue G7.) Pellingham, after a moment, says 'Well done, Lonnie,' and means it. Advantage if Lonnie already told the party at the depot.
skillChecks.failure: Lonnie cannot do it in front of Pellingham. He stares at his shoes. The party will need the hatbox itself, or Lonnie alone with Dolan later.

skillChecks.success: If Pellingham will not trade, a party member slips into his bedroom during the talk and finds the hatbox on the closet shelf (Clue G8), and can bring it out or leave it for Dolan. Rudd notices only on a natural 1.
skillChecks.failure: Rudd is standing in the bedroom doorway. 'Mr. Pellingham's room,' he says, politely. 'I'll ask you to stay out of it.'

encounters: No fight is planned in this act. Every person in the room is armed or has someone armed: Rudd (Bodyguard), Tiny Mulcahy (Mob Lieutenant), Larrabee (Waterfront Boss, who fights through others), Lonnie (Hired Gun stats; he will not fire), and Corinne, who has a Derringer in the vanity case beside the bonds

acts.title: Act 3: Fog at the Window
acts.description: The last half hour before midnight, and the morning after. Larrabee's man from Los Angeles comes up the service lift; Corinne runs for the scaffolding with the vanity case; and the party must decide what becomes of the bonds, the crane, and Corinne Marsh. There is no correct ending. There are several honest ones, listed in the campaign's control file.
objectives: Stop Corinne on the scaffold, or let her go
Decide what happens to the bonds
Decide what happens to the crane

scenes.name: The Service Lift
scenes.description: At about a quarter past eleven, whenever the room is at its most tense, the service lift in the pantry hums and opens, and Mr. Gray steps out: a small neat man in a grey suit with a .45 automatic and no expression. He came to collect what Larrabee is owed and has been told it is in the room. He is The Professional and the most dangerous person in the campaign, and he does not care about the crane, the bonds' owners, or anyone's speeches. Tiny Mulcahy, if the party won him on Market Street, steps aside and takes Larrabee by the arm.
scenes.readAloud: The lift in the pantry hums, and stops, and the gate folds back with a sound like a pair of shears. The man who steps out is small, and neat, and grey from his hat to his shoes, and he is holding a .45 automatic down by his leg the way another man might hold an umbrella. He looks round the room once, the way a surveyor looks at a field, and his eyes stop on the blue vanity case on Corinne Marsh's knee. 'Mr. Larrabee,' he says, pleasantly. 'Is that it?' And Larrabee, who looks suddenly ten years older, says, 'Now, Gray, wait a minute,' and Gray does not wait.

skillChecks.success: The party sees Gray's eyes go to the case, and has one action before he moves: a shove, a shot, a shout, Dolan out of the bedroom. Everyone else in the room rolls initiative normally.
skillChecks.failure: Gray fires first, at whoever is nearest the case. Roll initiative.

skillChecks.success: With Dolan out of the bedroom and his badge up, or with Gray hurt and three guns on him, Gray weighs the arithmetic, lowers the .45, and says, 'Not for six thousand.' He goes back down the lift. He is never seen in San Francisco again.
skillChecks.failure: Gray fights until he is down or until the arithmetic is very clear, then tries for the lift.

scenes.name: Nineteen Floors
scenes.description: In the chaos, Corinne Marsh goes out through the hinged boarding onto the builders' scaffold with the vanity case under her arm, along the wet planks toward the roof stairs, in heels, in fog, nineteen floors over California Street. Someone follows her or no one does. This is the campaign's last physical set piece: no fight, unless she draws the Derringer; a pursuit along a plank, a rope hoist, a case that might fall.
scenes.readAloud: The cold hits you first: the fog coming in through the open panel like breath, wet on your face. Then the drop. There is no street down there, only white, lit from underneath, and the plank under your feet is eleven inches wide and slick as a fish, and somewhere below in the white a cable car bell is ringing on California Street as if nothing were happening. Corinne is twenty feet ahead of you along the scaffold with one hand on the pipe rail and the blue case under her arm, and her fox has slipped off her shoulders and is hanging by one end over nothing. She looks back at you. Her face is wet. 'Let me go,' she says. 'For God's sake. You've got your bird.'

skillChecks.success: You close the distance along the plank. Each round on the scaffold a character who moves more than half speed makes this check; failure means a slip (DEX save DC 12 or fall to the next scaffold level, 2d6 bludgeoning, and a very bad second).
skillChecks.failure: You slip and catch the rail with one hand. Corinne gains ten feet.

skillChecks.success: Corinne stops. She is shaking with cold and fear, and she knows the stairs ahead are a dead end with Dolan's men on them. She holds out the case over the drop and says, 'Tell me why I shouldn't.' Give the player a moment to answer. If it is a good answer, she gives the case to them, and sits down on the wet plank in her grey gown, and lets them help her in.
skillChecks.failure: Corinne draws the Derringer from the case (+5 to hit, 1d6+3, two shots). She will fire if anyone comes within ten feet. The case may fall (DEX save DC 13 to catch it if she is shot or grabbed; if it falls, the bonds scatter across the roof of the Mark Hopkins' California Street wing, two floors down, and must be gathered in the fog).

skillChecks.success: The rope hoist: a character can swing out on the builders' rope and cut Corinne off at the roof stairs, landing between her and the door.
skillChecks.failure: The hoist rope runs out through the block. The character hangs over nineteen floors of fog and must be hauled back in.

scenes.name: Midnight
scenes.description: The penthouse after the fight, the scaffold and the shouting, at a few minutes to midnight. Dolan, Corinne (in custody or not), the bonds (in someone's hands), the crane (in someone's hands), Magda, Pellingham, Lonnie. The party makes its choices. Then the morning: Hattie at the microscope, a cable to Lisbon, a liner sailing from Pier 35 with or without cabin B-14's passenger, and on Monday a funeral at Holy Cross in Colma.
scenes.readAloud: The clock on the mantelpiece says four minutes to twelve. The fire has burned down. Somebody has closed the panel on the fog, and the room is very quiet: Dolan by the door with his hat in his hand, Lonnie on the sofa with his face in his hands, Mr. Pellingham in his great chair with the cracked crane in his lap like a sleeping cat, Magda at the window with her back to everyone. On the lacquer table, in the middle of the room, sit a blue leather vanity case and a black hatbox. Dolan looks at them, and then at you, and then at his watch. 'Well,' he says. 'It's not midnight yet. Tell me what happened here. Tell me all of it, and tell me what you want me to write down.'

skillChecks.success: Dolan agrees to let the bonds go to Magda Ehrlich's bank account on Monday morning, 'returned to the owner of record', and to keep them out of the evidence room, at the cost of his own rules. Advantage if the party has shown him the Friday papers' reports from Germany and Austria, or has been straight with him all week. He tears up the warrant for Cass Delaney either way, if he has Corinne and the gun.
skillChecks.failure: Dolan says the bonds are evidence and he will log them. 'Six months. A year. I'm sorry.' The party may take them anyway, before he logs them, if they choose. He will know. He may or may not say.

skillChecks.success: Pellingham, holding the crane, would give it back to Magda for nothing, tonight, if the party asked him in the right words; he has just watched a woman nearly die for what was in it, and something has moved in him. It will not move again. He may also simply pay Magda $11,500 for it, if she would rather have the money. She chooses.
skillChecks.failure: Pellingham holds the crane and says nothing. He has kept his part of any bargain he made.

skillChecks.success: Magda, turning from the window, says what she wants now that it is over, in her own words. Let the party hear it. Whatever they have chosen, she thanks them for one specific thing they did this week, and names it.
skillChecks.failure: Magda thanks them, simply, and asks to be taken to the Western Union office on Market Street, which is open all night.

Mick Larrabee (Waterfront Boss), who shouts 'Get him!' and expects others to do it; Tiny Mulcahy (Mob Lieutenant), who may refuse

npcsInvolved.name: Ambrose Pellingham, 58
npcsInvolved.role: Host; collector; holder of the gun
npcsInvolved.description: The most courteous man in the campaign at the most dangerous party in it. He proposes the devil's bargain because he genuinely believes it is the most civilised outcome, and he is not entirely wrong. Whatever he agrees to, he does.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The crane. A civilised settlement. And, a little, to see Corinne Marsh pay for the robbery.

npcsInvolved.name: Corinne Marsh, 42
npcsInvolved.description: Grey gown, silver fox, a blue leather vanity case with $38,000 in Treasury bearer bonds and a Derringer in it. Her fourth account is the nearest she comes to the truth. On the scaffold she is no longer acting.
npcsInvolved.motivation: The boat at nine. Then nothing at all, if she cannot have it.

npcsInvolved.name: Magda Ehrlich, 27
npcsInvolved.role: The client; owner of the crane by any decent reckoning
npcsInvolved.description: In the room by her own choice. She speaks rarely and every word lands. She makes her own decision about Pellingham's settlement and about the crane, and the party should hear it.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Her family, then Ned Corrigan, then the crane. She is ashamed of the order and will not change it.

npcsInvolved.name: Lonnie Pruitt, 21
npcsInvolved.description: A glass of milk in his hand, a new hat on his knee. Whether he speaks depends on whether anyone stands next to him.
npcsInvolved.motivation: To tell the truth once in front of the man who frightens him most, and go home.

npcsInvolved.name: Mick Larrabee, 50
npcsInvolved.description: Comes for his money and has sent for a man he cannot control. Finds out, too late, what he has done.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Six thousand dollars and his face.

npcsInvolved.name: Tiny Mulcahy, 34
npcsInvolved.description: If the party won him in the two minutes' silence, he steps out of the fight and takes Larrabee's arm, and says 'That's enough, Mick.'
npcsInvolved.motivation: To go home to Daly City without anybody's blood on him.

npcsInvolved.name: Mr. Gray, age unknown
npcsInvolved.description: Small, neat, grey, polite, a .45 automatic held like an umbrella. No history, no speech, no interest in anything but the case on Corinne's knee. He is the only person in the campaign with no story, and that is the point of him.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His fee. He will weigh it against the odds and leave if the arithmetic is bad.

npcsInvolved.name: Mr. Rudd, 40
npcsInvolved.description: A former Philadelphia policeman in a good suit, quiet, loyal, unimpressed by anybody. Protects Pellingham and nobody else.
npcsInvolved.motivation: His employer's safety and his own professional pride.

npcsInvolved.name: Lieutenant Frank Dolan, 47
npcsInvolved.description: Behind the bedroom door, or through the front door at midnight. In the end he is the person the party must tell the truth to, and he decides, as much as they do, what that truth is worth.
npcsInvolved.motivation: Ned's killer in a cell. A case that stands up. And, by the end, perhaps something more than his rules.

rewards.money: Pellingham's settlement, if accepted: $5,000 to the agency. Otherwise, Magda's $5,000 finder's fee from the Ehrlich bonds if they reach her bank by the 18th; Pellingham's $1,000 reward if he ends with the crane; and Ned Corrigan's key-man policy, $5,000 to Cass Delaney, which the insurer pays in December once Dolan closes the case. Mr. Gray carries $300 and a return ticket on the Daylight.
items: Clues G7 and G8, and with them the whole case against Corinne Marsh
The Colt .32 automatic, serial 482117, for Dolan, or for the bay
The blue leather vanity case: $38,000 in United States Treasury bearer bonds and a Derringer with .41 rounds (2)
The Black Crane, cracked, to whoever the story gives it
A letter from Dr. Otto Ehrlich, from New York, in January 1939, if the family gets out; it encloses a photograph of four people on a ship's deck
Cass Delaney's agency license, renewed, if Dolan closes the case

twists: Pellingham's settlement is not a trick. It would work. Everyone would be paid and nobody would hang. The only cost is that Ned's killer walks away with nineteen thousand dollars of a refugee family's money and a pistol to drop in the bay. Let the players feel how reasonable it is.

Corinne's fourth account explains the clue players found on the first night: the fox hairs on Ned's right sleeve and the lighter in his hand. She let him light her cigarette, the one time all week she let any man do it, to bring him close. A table that remembers she always lights her own (bc-scenario-001, Vallejo Street) will see the whole murder in that one gesture.

Mr. Gray is the only person in the campaign with no story and no wants beyond his fee. He comes because of a decision Larrabee made in anger, and he is the cost of a world in which everyone has been trading all week. If the party survives him, the rest is talk.

Pellingham, at the very end, may give the crane back to Magda. He is a vulture, and he has watched a woman nearly die on a plank for what was inside his bird, and once in his life it moves him. Do not make it a conversion. It is one gesture, and he will be buying a Viennese doctor's silver at a tenth of its value in Lisbon by March.

Dolan's choice is as much the ending as the party's. A lieutenant who lets $38,000 of evidence go to a refugee's bank account on Monday morning is breaking his rules for the first time in twenty years. Let him do it, or not, according to how the party has treated him all week.
dmTips: This is a drawing-room scene, and it should feel like one. Seat everyone. Give each person in the room one line in the first ten minutes. Let Pellingham run it like a hostess until the party takes it away from him.

Let the players make the case. Do not narrate the reveal for them. Prompt with the Case Board if they need it, and have the room react to each clue: Larrabee laughing at the cable car, Magda closing her eyes at the gloves, Lonnie flinching at the ash can, Pellingham nodding at each one like a man watching a good hand of bridge.

Mr. Gray is a deliberately dangerous fight for 6th-level characters. He has no allies in the room and he wants the case, not a massacre. Use him to break the stalemate, not to kill the party: he fires at whoever is nearest the case, and he leaves when the arithmetic turns. If the party has Dolan in the bedroom and Tiny on their side, the fight should be short.
The scaffold is a pursuit, not a fight. Corinne is not a gunfighter and does not want to die. Give the player who follows her the last real conversation in the campaign.

Every ending in the control file is honest. Do not punish the party for accepting Pellingham's settlement, or for taking the bonds out from under Dolan, or for letting Corinne reach the boat. Play the consequences, quietly, in the epilogue: who comes to the funeral, what Dolan says at the graveside, whether there is a letter from New York in January.
Level-up note: award the 9,000 XP in this file at midnight. Each character reaches 7th level (23,000 XP).

The epilogue: Saturday morning, the liner sailing from Pier 35 with or without cabin B-14's passenger; Hattie at her microscope at noon, saying 'Match' to nobody; the Western Union counter on Market Street; and on Monday 14 November, Ned Corrigan's funeral at Holy Cross in Colma, in the fog, with Dot and Dolan and Rose and Hattie and Benny, and everyone the party has met who has a reason to come. Read it slowly. It is the last scene.
